general.temas: Recurring topics include diplomacy and China’s relations with the United States, international cooperation, the environment and advanced technologies. CGTN and South China Morning Post also highlight issues related to APEC. Only Xinhua devotes several headlines to COVID-19, with reports on vaccination, prevention and commercial reopening.
general.motivo_crispacion: Tensions center on protests in the United States against attacks on Iran, a Chinese expert’s criticism of the Philippines, and a US plan that could affect Chinese laboratories. A possible corruption case in China and an investigation into chip exports also feature. News of diplomatic dialogue, environmental protection and technological advances offers a calmer contrast. The front pages refer to different dates, so they do not necessarily reflect the same day.

Diario del Pueblo.resumen:
- Several stories highlight environmental protection and Xi Jinping’s initiatives to mark World Environment Day.
- The government addresses the summer harvest and announces an agricultural census for 2026.
- Han Zheng receives an unofficial US dialogue delegation.
- Rules on military facilities and Party discipline are published, and the implementation of the energy conservation law is reviewed.
- Other stories cover the university entrance exam, traditional tea-making and Xi’s recent activities.
Diario del Pueblo.motivo_populismo: The headlines use emotive and promotional expressions such as “protect mountains and rivers,” “lifeline” and “move the world,” but do not frame the issue as a conflict between the people and the elites.
Diario del Pueblo.sesgo: The front page prioritizes the institutional perspective and presents Xi Jinping’s leadership and official initiatives favorably. Critical voices or alternative perspectives are barely represented.

Xinhua.resumen:
- The front page highlights changes in China and the years three astronauts spent preparing.
- It reports on commercial reopening and a plan for a second COVID-19 booster dose.
- It offers advice for older people and cardiovascular patients, and addresses questions about asymptomatic infection data.
- It includes information on the BQ.1 variant and warns of a new cold snap.
- It covers Xi Jinping’s diplomatic activities, a planned speech on biodiversity and financial oversight proposals.
Xinhua.motivo_populismo: The headlines are mostly informative, although some use questions and formulations such as “6, 10, 12 years” to arouse curiosity; there is no discernible conflict between the people and the elites.
Xinhua.sesgo: The selection gives prominence to health measures and the decisions and activities of the authorities, presented from an institutional perspective. It also highlights a positive image of China’s development.

Global Times.resumen:
- Analysts warn that a US FCC plan concerning Chinese laboratories could disrupt supply chains and raise costs.
- A Chinese expert criticizes a Philippine statement about an agreement with Japan; another headline questions the narrative of Yasukuni Shrine.
- The front page covers protests in the US against attacks on Iran, as well as news of a shooting in Washington and a commemorative event in South Africa.
- China announces new train timetables and expects another lunar mission this year; its prospects in artificial intelligence and multilateralism are also highlighted.
- It reports on visits from Taiwan to mainland China and a proposal to add sex education to the school curriculum.
Global Times.motivo_populismo: Although informative headlines predominate, expressions such as “hidden motives,” “inverted narrative” and “more chaos” add a confrontational and alarmist tone.
Global Times.sesgo: The selection presents China’s development and international role favorably, while highlighting criticism and problems linked to the United States, Japan and the Philippines. It also includes social and infrastructure issues presented in an informative manner.

CGTN.resumen:
- Innovation in Suzhou highlights robots, precision tools and smart factories.
- China takes part in COP31 and calls for dialogue to reduce tensions in Yemen and the Red Sea.
- Several stories address cooperation in APEC and BRICS and dialogue between China and the United States.
- Xi Jinping calls for honoring Sun Yat-sen’s legacy in pursuit of “national rejuvenation.”
- Other pieces cover traditional fishing, technology in Shenzhen and literary journeys through China.
CGTN.motivo_populismo: An informative tone predominates, although expressions such as “the great dream of all the Chinese people” and “remarkable achievements” add emotive and celebratory emphasis.
CGTN.sesgo: The selection offers a favorable view of Chinese initiatives and diplomacy, with an emphasis on innovation, cooperation and national achievements. No critical perspectives are apparent in the texts provided.

South China Morning Post.resumen:
- Shenzhen is finalizing security preparations for APEC; contacts between China, South Korea, the United States and Russia are announced.
- Artificial intelligence detects a possible corruption case in Wuhan, and the Chinese military turns to data to improve its recruitment.
- Scientists are fired after the death of a girl in a gene-editing trial; another study links tight underwear to erectile dysfunction.
- The front page addresses Chinese patents for underwater data centers and proposes sharing the country’s experience in renewable energy.
- It also covers tensions surrounding the High Seas Treaty and the US investigation into Nvidia and chip exports to China.
South China Morning Post.motivo_populismo: An informative tone predominates, although expressions such as “the devils in the details” and “sex scandal” resort to sensationalism, without an explicit conflict between the people and the elites.
South China Morning Post.sesgo: The selection presents international affairs from a China-centered perspective, with attention to technology, security and its global role. It combines favorable news about Chinese advances with critical reports on corruption, security controls and scientific research.

opiniones.comunista:
I see a question of class in environmental news: who decides what happens to land, energy and water, and for whose benefit? Protecting nature cannot be reduced to a slogan while big capital retains the power to turn the commons into private profit. I support collective ownership and democratic management of those resources, with effective participation by those who work with them and depend on them for their livelihoods.

The announcement of a new agricultural census and the attention to the harvest offer an opportunity to direct planning toward the needs of the peasantry and food security, rather than profits for a few. The same applies to energy: oversight of the conservation law must be accompanied by public investment and accessible services. A just ecological transition is measured by the life it guarantees the working majority.
opiniones.anarquista:
I think it is right that environmental protection should make the front pages, but I distrust its presentation as a task directed from above. Those who cultivate the land and inhabit these territories should be able to decide how to care for them, share resources and coordinate freely, without being subordinated to the priorities of a party or the state. Self-management does not eliminate the need for cooperation: it makes cooperation accountable to those who live with its consequences.

I am also troubled that, to prepare for the APEC meetings in Shenzhen, some residents have been asked to leave their homes. If the stability of summits requires sacrificing people’s everyday freedom, whom does that stability serve? I prefer cooperation built from the bottom up, through mutual aid and free agreements, to governance that reserves decisions for those in power.
opiniones.liberal:
News about environmental protection and food security raises legitimate goals: we all want clean air and available food. But I doubt that central planning is the best answer. When farmers and businesses can decide, invest and compete, they have incentives to find solutions suited to their needs. The state should enforce clear rules against pollution, not direct every productive activity.

I am also concerned about the US proposal to exclude Chinese laboratories from electronics testing. Raising barriers to trade can make products more expensive and penalize consumers in both countries. I prefer dialogue and open markets to suspicion turned into economic policy.

Prosperity requires individual freedom, responsibility for harm caused and a limited state, financed by low taxes that leave more resources in the hands of those who generate them.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
I see a lesson in these front pages that the West would do well to heed: sovereignty requires producing food, protecting territory and preserving inherited knowledge. China’s attention to the harvest and its rural traditions points to something essential: a nation that abandons its countryside loses security and continuity. Protecting nature also means defending the homeland we will leave to our children, not merely following international slogans.

But I distrust a press that turns every official initiative into a tribute to power. Discipline and planning are no substitute for accountability. Dialogue between China and the United States can be useful, provided cooperation is not confused with strategic dependence. I prefer governments that negotiate from a position of strength and answer to their citizens, not to elites pleased with their own statements.
opiniones.centro:
I see an opportunity in dialogue between China and the United States: keeping channels open does not require ignoring differences, but preventing every disagreement from becoming a crisis. Trade and technological cooperation need clear rules and sustained negotiations, not gestures that raise costs without assessing their consequences.

I also welcome the space given to environmental protection in the news. But commitments must translate into verifiable rules and a transition that does not leave workers and rural communities to fend for themselves. The market can drive innovation, while institutions set limits and protect those who bear the costs.

Finally, the case of the girl who died in a gene-editing trial is a reminder that scientific ambition is not enough: independent oversight, transparency and safeguards for patients are needed.
